title: One Penguin Group Stays Steady While Its Neighbor Shrinks
summary:
Two groups of rare penguins live on far-off islands near New Zealand, and their stories are very different. One group has stayed about the same size for at least 25 years, while the other has shrunk by more than 40 percent.

The birds are Erect-crested penguins. They breed nowhere else on Earth except the Bounty and Antipodes islands, about 800 kilometres southeast of New Zealand's South Island. Researchers from the University of Otago used drone surveys between 2022 and 2024 to count every breeding colony.

The tiny Bounty Islands, covering just 50 hectares, hold about 27,800 breeding pairs. That is almost as many as the Antipodes Islands, with about 29,800 pairs, even though the Antipodes are 40 times larger.

Scientists think several things may be behind the split. Skuas eat penguin eggs and chicks, and they may do more harm as colonies shrink. Eastern Rockhopper penguins have nearly vanished from the Antipodes, with fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs left, so skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguins instead. Strong storms have also caused landslides that break up breeding colonies.
why_it_matters: Learning why one penguin group is shrinking helps us protect wild animals before they disappear, just like looking after the nature near your own home.

background_read: Erect-crested penguins are rare penguins that breed only on the Bounty and Antipodes islands near New Zealand.
Penguins return to the same islands each year to raise their chicks, and counting them shows whether their numbers are growing or shrinking.
Scientists study these island penguins to learn what is helping some groups stay steady and what is putting others at risk.
